rationale: B wins because it protects the founder from the trap A keeps stepping into: pretending the robot explains the price freeze. B explicitly kills "Robots are paying for Chipotle's price freeze" as a hallucinated fact, while A leads with "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" and later says "Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices." That is the difference between a skeptical story a reporter can test and a company-friendly claim that invites the takedown.
gaps_in_A: "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" asserts a causal link the update does not provide. The body later caveats it, but the headline already spent the credibility.
"Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices" is worse: the update says Chipotle is rolling out Autocado and holding prices flat, not that Chipotle says robots justify the freeze.
"Its Competitors Are Taking Notes" invents competitor reaction. No competitor, analyst, or operator evidence was supplied.
"layered approach to kitchen orchestration" inflates one 100-store rollout plus one unspecified test into category architecture. That may become true, but the proof is not in the update.
gaps_in_B: "100 robot-equipped stores out of more than 3,500 cannot offset chain-wide food-cost inflation" is plausible, but it still needs cost data before being treated as arithmetic fact.
"The prevailing belief is that chains pass food-cost inflation straight to the menu" is useful framing, but unsourced. Do not smuggle market consensus in through the side door.
"This beat has watched kitchen robots stall at the demo stage" is good reporter context only if backed with examples; the company update does not supply it.
